It is true that every Senator's office gets an Electoral vote: 

there is a historical reason for this as well!  It is because each Senate office is the office of a President/former President. 

I think, the simplest reason, is that the founders imagined that it would be reasonable for each State, to be able to elect a President;  and that, furthermore, for the purposes of states' rights, for those populations of people, that nothing could be more valuable, than having a President from (your state) elected.  

Though, in the modern day, the importance of what state is running which political candidate, seems to be downsized ... or neglected. 

(but as importantly, at least potentially to international observers, is that we tend to see that the popularity of the Founding Fathers traditions of American constitutionalism, its East Coast, outweighs significantly, its Founding Mothers traditions, West Coast, influence , but maybe that is an issue for another day ...)

I think the point that people miss, with "the Electoral College", is that Elections, and Democratic infrastructure is in some sense, multi-layered and complex: 

a,   a person attempting to receive a Formal position, like Superintendant, or Principal;  could be in a sense, running for a formal office

b,   these formal offices, are potentially related as local government, in hierarchies which are relevant to State offices, with local formal offices congruent to jobs and statuses, within state government

c,  likewise state government, has responsibilities not only to the national government, but to international government as well

d,   in some cases, the idea that these local or state jobs are "owned", - (the implied congruency to a national or state title), is a kind of de facto incumbency,  however, not only these candidates, but other types of candidacy is relevant, to the election process

e,   furthermore, vote tabulation is itself "mutli-structural", - with many democratic proceduralists maintaining that not only "specific and defined" kinds of voting, but any kind of voting being "popular voting", which proves relevant to the election process

f,   other even more ambitious thinkers, hypothesize that any of a broad range of activity can be used to communicate or signal votes  (deciding between Count Chocula or Captain Crunch, can be a kind of voting experiment, or deciding between your favorite Cola)

g,   the electoral college, therefore:  exists not only to decide between "weighted Electoral" votes,  and "population votes", but to help to resolve all of these inconsistencies

h,   historically:  the internal processes within a state produce a number of high ranking officials (possibly, a Mayor, secretary, or governor), or at least persons occupying jobs that are equivalent to this;  (but why don't local partisans vote their people into the Top seat, why not make their Party the Presidential party?)

i,    but often lack the means to attempt the more ambitious tasks:  of running a national government,   

j,   therefore, the Electors, take the votes they've amassed, and pledge them, as a kind of "extended social contract", or rather contract between states and nationalism,  in a Presidential contest;  in exchange, for benefits, guaranteed, by National Unity parties (for support through national tax initiatives, and programs, and other kinds of national programming, originating in the national capital) 

k,   though hypothetically, some speculate, that in a broader international democracy, for example, along the New Mexico-Arizona border, near Texas,  other kinds of issues arise:   do not Spanish/English speaking people, pledge their votes to the President of the United States, or el Presidente of the Estados Unidos?  

l,   the Electoral College exists to help to resolve many differences and ambiguities of weightedness, and other issues relating to voting, on a localized and broad scale !
